svg.title: Lateral and directional stability: what makes the airplane self-righting
svg.desc: Four lateral stability design factors: dihedral, sweepback, keel effect and weight distribution. Dihedral: outer wing tips higher than the roots; in a sideslip the wing slipping into the wind has more AOA and lift, which raises the windward wing. As a rough estimate 10 degrees of sweepback gives about 1 degree of effective dihedral and a high wing gives about 5 degrees more than a low wing. Sweepback: the low wing presents its leading edge more perpendicular to the airflow, gains lift and rises. Keel effect: the fuselage acts like a keel, with most keel area above the CG, and its weight acts like a pendulum. Directional stability: more side area aft of the CG than ahead plus a vertical fin makes the airplane act like a weather vane; the pilot must reestablish the original heading. Drawings are schematic.
svg.text: Lateral and directional stability: what makes the airplane self-righting
Lateral (rolling) stability has four design factors: dihedral, sweepback, keel effect and weight
distribution. Directional (yawing) stability comes mostly from the fin. Drawings are schematic.
Dihedral
tip higher than root
rear view, nose toward you (schematic)
Outer wing tips higher than the wing roots
A gust rolls the airplane and the sideslip brings
the relative wind from the side: the wing slipping
into the wind has more AOA and lift, the other wing
less
The change in lift gives a rolling moment that
raises the windward wing: stable roll due to
sideslip
Rough estimates: 10 degrees of sweepback gives
about 1 degree of effective dihedral; a high wing
gives about 5 degrees more effective dihedral than
a low wing
Sweepback
leading edge
slopes backward
top view (schematic)
flight
A swept wing has its leading edge sloping backward
When a wing drops or slips, the low wing presents
its leading edge more perpendicular to the relative
airflow: more lift, it rises, and the attitude is
restored
In a yaw, the forward wing gets more airspeed and
drag and pulls back toward the original path; this
contribution to directional stability is small
Keel effect and weight distribution
CG
greater part of the keel area is above the CG
side view (schematic)
A high wing airplane tends to turn its longitudinal
axis into the relative wind (keel effect); the
fuselage acts like a keel, steadying it
When one wing dips, the fuselage weight acts like a
pendulum returning the airplane to level
Slipping to one side: weight plus airflow pressure
on the upper keel area, both acting about the CG,
roll the airplane back to wings level
Directional stability: fin and fuselage
CG (pivot)
less side area ahead
greater side area aft
fin
top view, weather vane idea (schematic)
Directional stability is yawing stability about the
vertical axis; the most easily achieved stability
in design
Side surface greater aft than ahead of the CG, plus
a vertical fin: the airplane points its nose into
the relative wind like a weather vane or arrow
The farther aft and the larger the fin, the greater
the directional stability
The restoring tendency is slow and ends when the
skid ends; the airplane does not return to the
original heading by itself and the pilot must
reestablish it
